quote: But if you keep the hammer and use it to drive nails, who can doubt its worth?
content: The koan's test is the right one, and it has not been applied. The claim that the sequence's techniques drive nails, that people trained in them make better decisions or more accurate judgments than people who are not, is an empirical claim that could be measured with the tools the book describes, and in the years since it was written the only attempt was a small, unreviewed, self-report survey run by the community's own training organization, which found modest changes in reported wellbeing and nothing about accuracy. The debiasing literature that exists, reviewed in the annotations to Knowing About Biases Can Hurt People, finds that awareness-based training of the kind the sequence offers has little effect. Ougi tells the novice to stop asking whether it is a cult and see whether the hammer works. Two decades on, the master's own school has not looked.
